question: Ms. Reyes is planning a two-week unit that introduces about forty new words for food and cooking. She wants her students to still know the words at the end of the term, not only at the end of the week. Her draft plan presents all forty words in the first two lessons through picture-and-translation slides, then moves on to other content and expects students to review the lists at home. Drawing on what the course teaches about how vocabulary is learned and how lessons are planned, what should Ms. Reyes change about her plan, and why?
answer: Ms. Reyes's draft relies on the two weakest methods the vocabulary research identifies: massed presentation of all forty words at once, followed by re-reading the lists at home. Karpicke and Roediger (2008) showed that after a first correct recall further study adds nothing while further retrieval keeps strengthening memory, and spaced practice reliably beats massed practice (Nakata 2015; Kim and Webb 2022, 48 experiments, 3,411 participants). She should introduce the words in smaller batches and build short, spaced retrieval events into the plan across the two weeks and beyond, writing the review into the lesson sequence rather than delegating it to unstructured home study.
anchor: Karpicke and Roediger (2008) demonstrated that once a learner has recalled a word correctly once, further study of that word produces no measurable gain in retention at one week, while further retrieval continues to strengthen it.
